title: [Chapitre] IX et IX bis. [Ateliers] : notes manuscrites (05-15/07/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Context (from previous and next pages): Grothendieck is building a combinatorial model of 'constructible' subsets of a one-dimensional object, an interval I with endpoints ∂I = {ω0, ω1}. M is a set of 'objects': the points a and the open intervals I_{a,b}. A 'découpage' (cutting) T is a finite subdivision of I into vertices and open intervals, and Φ_T is its set of cells. A 'polygon' is a union of cells of some T. The map Φ ↦ S_Φ sends sets of cells to constructible parts Σ_cons(M); on the previous page he checks that it is compatible with complement and intersection, which gives a support axiom 'Atsupp 1'. Two polygons Φ, Ψ are 'commensurable' when δΦ ∪ δΨ (their boundary points) generates a découpage.

This page:
(1) Commensurable polygons are subordinate to a common découpage δΦ ∪ δΨ ∪ ∂I = T, i.e. they have a common refinement. The same holds for any finite family of polygons or constructible parts, possibly after subdividing intervals, which does not change the parts.
(2) Hence all usual operations on a finite family of mutually commensurable elements of Σ_cons reduce to ∪, ∩ and complement inside a suitable finite Boolean algebra P(Φ_T).
(3) Count: if T has n intervals and n+1 vertices, then card Φ_T = 2n+1. So there are 2^{2n+1} parts subordinate to T.
(4) He begins case (2): an interval where the endpoints ω0, ω1 are not given. It is to be deduced from the case (I, ∂I) by taking a 'residual' or complementary set at one or both ends. The next page develops this as an ordered set J = I \ {ω0} with a greatest element ω1, using the objects a, J_{<a} and J_{a,b}.

In modern terms, the Boolean algebra of constructible (definable) subsets of a one-dimensional ordered set is the filtered colimit, over finite cell decompositions, of the finite Boolean algebras P(cells). This is the elementary one-dimensional cell-decomposition picture familiar from o-minimality and stratified/tame topology. Its purpose seems to be to set up axioms for supports and cosupports ('Omb', supp, cosupp) for a combinatorial theory of 'ateliers'.
errors: The transcription says 'n intervalles et n sommets', but card Φ_T = 2n+1 requires n+1 vertices (endpoints included). Either the image reads n+1 or this is a slip; the stated cardinality 2n+1 is correct with n+1 vertices.
Commensurability as defined (δΦ ∪ δΨ is a découpage) only makes sense for finitely many polygons. The remark extending it to 'un ensemble quelconque' should be read as 'any finite family'.

ideas.what: Common refinement of cell decompositions; finite families of constructible sets live in a finite Boolean algebra P(Φ_T)
ideas.modern_name: Constructible/definable Boolean algebra as a filtered colimit of finite Boolean algebras of cells (1-dim cell decomposition)
ideas.usually_credited_to: folklore; o-minimal cell decomposition (van den Dries, Pillay–Steinhorn, Knight 1980s)
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme only alludes to 'topologie modérée' in general

ideas.what: Counting cells: n intervals and n+1 vertices give 2n+1 cells and 2^{2n+1} subordinate parts
ideas.modern_name: elementary combinatorics of a subdivided interval

ideas.what: Interval without marked endpoints obtained from (I, ∂I) by removing an endpoint, i.e. an ordered set J with a maximum
ideas.modern_name: half-open/open intervals as complements of strata; pointed-interval combinatorics

deep.surprise_reason: This is routine bookkeeping on Boolean algebras of cells of a subdivided interval, in service of a larger axiomatic project (supports and cosupports in 'ateliers'). The page itself contains nothing new.
transcription_corrections: Line 1 is likely 'sont subordonnés (ou « subdivisions ») à un même découpage', rather than 'rapport ssm'.
'une famille quelconque d'objets étendus de Σ_con' is probably 'une famille quelconque d'éléments de Σ_cons'.
'n sommets' should probably read 'n+1 sommets', consistent with card Φ_T = 2n+1.
'diédrite' is probably 'déduit': 'On doit le voir comme déduit du cas précédent (I, ∂I)'.
'Cas où T de longueur n' is plausibly 'CAS où T de longueur n'.
